title: Retain a housing in a rollover fixture, turn it over and lock it, and fit a pad on its far face
instruction: Lay the housing in the rollover fixture with its orange recess down, slide the blue bar across it, turn the fixture over, push the red bolt home, fit the white wear pad in the recess, and move both hands away.
context: Assemblies such as engines and gearboxes are held in rollover stands and turned over to reach their undersides. The work has to be secured before it is inverted, and the stand locked before anyone works on it.
setup:
An assembly bench with a small rollover fixture on it. Fixture measurements are in the README ("Fixture dimensions"); in brief, with x and y as below and heights above the table, level at the start. A dark steel base 14 x 23.5 x 0.6 cm (x 22 to 36, y -13.5 to 10) carries two steel pillars 6 cm wide in x (x 26 to 32) and 1.2 cm thick in y: the near one at y -12 to -10.8, 8.7 cm tall; the far one at y 7.2 to 8.4, 11.5 cm tall, with a 1.2 cm gap at 9.4 to 10.6 cm height for the bolt. The base is fixed to the table in the simulation (a fixed joint to the world). On a real table, bolt it down, or hold it with two low toe clamps on the strips of the base 1.5 cm wide outside the cradle's footprint (x 22 to 23.5 and 34.5 to 36; clamps under 1 cm tall, since the turning cradle's lowest point is 1.3 cm above the table), mid-length, clear of the pillars, bolt and crank.

A horizontal axle along y at x 29 cm, 7.5 cm above the table, is a 1.6 cm stub on each of the cradle's end plates (y -10.8 to -10.6 and 6.8 to 7.2) turning in its pillar; the simulation draws the stubs square and uses a hinge joint for the bearings. On a real fixture the near stub is a round 1.6 cm shaft that runs through a bore in the near pillar (close running fit) and carries the crank, clamped with a set screw, and the far stub turns in a bore in the far pillar. On the axle is an aluminium cradle: two rails 9.2 cm apart, each 0.8 cm thick in x and 5.1 cm tall (4.4 to 9.5 cm high), y -9.8 to 5.8; two ledges 1.6 cm wide and 5 mm thick (4.4 to 4.9 cm high) inside them, y -4.1 to 4.1, leaving a 6 cm wide opening between the ledges, closed at each end by a 6 mm thick beam across the cradle (y 4.1 to 4.7 and -4.7 to -4.1); on the beams, four corner stubs 2.4 cm in x, 6 mm in y and 8 mm tall (4.9 to 5.7 cm high) stop a housing along y, 8.2 cm apart; a near end plate 10.8 x 0.8 x 5.1 cm (y -10.6 to -9.8) and a far end plate 8 cm wide, 1 cm thick (y 5.8 to 6.8), 9 cm tall (3 to 12 cm high). It starts level, resting on its near stop, and its far stop is at 195 degrees, past turned over; in the simulation the stops are the hinge joint's limits; on a real fixture, a 4 mm pin fixed in the near pillar's inner face, 1.6 cm below the axle, runs in a 5 mm wide, 195 degree arc slot cut in the near end plate about the axle, and the slot's ends stop the cradle at 0 and at 195 degrees.

A dark crank 5.6 x 0.6 x 1.6 cm, 4 cm from the axle to the knob's centre, at the -y end (y -12.8 to -12.2) carries a yellow knob, a plastic 3 x 2.4 x 4 cm sleeve at y -14.6 cm (y -15.8 to -13.4, 5.5 to 9.5 cm high) that turns freely on its pin (the simulation draws a square sleeve touching the pin's end; on a real fixture the pin is 3 cm long, passes through a round bore in the knob and is held by a retaining clip); at the start the knob is on the near side, level with the axle at x 25 cm.

A blue aluminium retaining bar 9.1 x 3 x 0.8 cm (8.4 to 9.2 cm high) with a lug 4 cm wide, 0.8 cm thick and up to 12.5 cm high on its crank side fits between the inner faces of the two rails (0.5 mm of clearance each side) and slides 7.5 cm along y, from parked toward the crank (y -9 to -6) to its stop over the centre of the cradle (y -1.5 to 1.5), leaving 5 mm of play above a housing on the ledges. On a real fixture two 3 mm pins in each end of the bar, 2 cm apart, run in a 3.2 mm wide slot in each rail's inner face (8.8 cm high, y -8.65 to 1.15, so the pin centres travel y -8.5 to 1), which guides the bar, keeps it in when the cradle is turned over and sets its travel; the simulation uses a sliding joint with the same travel.

A red aluminium lock bolt 1.2 cm square and 5.6 cm long (y 7.4 to 13), 10 cm above the table in the +y pillar's gap, with a lug 4 cm wide whose top is 14.5 cm above the table, slides 1.5 cm along -y. On a real fixture two blocks in the pillar's gap, 1.2 cm apart, make the gap a square guide hole, and a vertical cross pin through the pillar's upper block runs in a 1.5 cm slot in the top of the bolt and sets its travel; the simulation uses a sliding joint. It can only enter a 1.6 cm wide, 3 cm tall notch (3 to 6 cm high, open at the bottom edge) in the cradle's far end plate within about 4.6 degrees of turned over; otherwise the plate stops it after 6 mm.

An aluminium housing 8 x 7 x 3 cm, 400 g, stands at (17, 24) cm with an orange recess 6 x 4 cm and 8 mm deep in its underside, facing down; its other faces are bare metal except an orange band around the bottom 1.1 cm. A white acetal wear pad 5 x 3 x 3 cm, 63 g, stands at (27, 26) cm. Positions are from the arm bases' midpoint in x and the table's centre line in y, with +y toward the left arm. The screenshot shows the start. A dimensioned plan and side view of the fixture, in mm, is in fixture_dimensions.svg in the task folder, with a table of every part in the README.
scoring: Read at the end of the run. A hand is a gripper's fingertip midpoint, and a part counts as let go only with both hands 6 cm or more from its box, in its own frame. 0 for good if the fixture turns past 30 degrees without the housing in the cradle and the bar closed, if the pad is in the recess before the bolt is home, or if a part leaves the table. In the cradle: the housing's underside centre within 12 mm across the cradle and 11 mm along it, 1.9 to 2.8 cm from the axle's level in the cradle's own axes, and its own up within 10 degrees of the cradle's, so a housing loaded upside down earns nothing. Bar closed: 7 cm or more of travel. Turned over: within 6 degrees of 180. Bolt home: 1.2 cm or more of travel. Pad in: within 7 mm of the recess's centre along each of the housing's sides, its base within 5 mm of the recess floor, and within 10 degrees of pointing out of the recess. Otherwise 0.2 for the housing in the cradle and let go; 0.4 with the bar closed as well; 0.6 also turned over; 0.8 also with the bolt home; 0.9 also with the pad in and let go; 1.0 also with both hands 6 cm or more from the housing, the pad, the knob and the bolt's lug, and all at rest (parts under 1 cm/s and 0.5 rad/s, the cradle under 3 degrees/s, bar and bolt under 1 cm/s) for the last 1 s.
reset_notes: Set the cradle level, withdraw the bar and bolt, and put the housing and pad back on the table. Nothing is consumed.
fidelity: A rigid-body simulation. The bar and bolt stay where pushed through joint damping alone, with no latch or detent modelled. The knob is a free sleeve, so a top-down hand needn't turn. The cradle's balance is set by hand and its stops are joint limits. The bolt enters its notch by real contact, and without the bar the housing really falls out. Parts are boxes with 5 to 6 mm of play, and the pad is only set in place, not fastened.
